source.title: Traite complet de l'art du chant
source.author: Manuel Garcia
source.section: On the emission of the voice (Part I, 1840; Part II, 1847)

guidance: Garcia — the first great scientist of the voice — has the singer take breath slowly and quietly, then begin the tone cleanly and exactly on pitch: no breathy leak before the note, no slam, and no sliding up into it. Practice single sustained vowels at a comfortable volume, giving all your attention to the first instant of each note; the onset sets the quality of everything that follows it.
note: The pd status covers the French original (1840/1847). English translations — notably the 1975 Paschke edition, A Complete Treatise on the Art of Singing — are largely still in copyright: do not quote translations verbatim.

source.title: Theoretical and Practical Vocal Method
source.author: Mathilde Marchesi
source.section: On the registers of the voice

guidance: Marchesi's method treats the register break as something to be crossed gently and often, never forced: chest voice is not pushed upward past its comfortable limit, and exercises that cross the passaggio are sung softly, letting the voice turn over early rather than late. If your top notes strain or the break announces itself, sing slow scales through that area quietly, thinking of thinning the sound before the break arrives instead of muscling through it.

source.title: Vocal Wisdom: Maxims of Giovanni Battista Lamperti
source.author: Giovanni Battista Lamperti (transcribed by William Earl Brown)

guidance: There is a whole tradition on this collected in Vocal Wisdom, the book of Lamperti's teaching: the tone rides on a steady, springy column of breath — appoggio — with the inhale muscles staying gently engaged while you sing, so the sound does not collapse as the phrase spends its air. If your pitch sags on sustained notes or phrase endings cave in, practice medium-length notes and make the last second as supported as the first. The breath maxims in your own copy are the place to go.

source.title: Fifty Lessons for the Voice, Op. 9
source.author: Giuseppe Concone

guidance: Concone's Fifty Lessons are the classic legato gym: sing them on a single pure vowel, connecting every note into one seamless line — no little h re-attacks between notes, no bump at the barline, the breath flowing evenly through the whole phrase. If your lines come out as separate beads instead of a thread, take an early Concone lesson far under tempo and refuse to let the vowel stop between pitches.
